Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual ARC interaction

1. Parse the grid, demos, and remaining budgets, and form a rule that explains both the changed cells and cells that stay unchanged. Treat each instance as fresh unless task context supplies reusable evidence.
2. Validate candidate rules cell-by-cell against every demo, including unchanged cells, dimensions, colors, and positions. Treat every distinctive arrangement as a possible *whole motif/template*, not merely a count of clue-colored cells: test exact shape and orientation/rotation/reflection, and locate matching occurrences before generalizing. Separately test whether the transformation instead uses lines, selected segments, intersections, or another subset. For line-pattern tasks, test row, column, `row-column`, and `row+column` invariants separately; distinguish line extension, motif repetition, and other effects. When output dimensions are integer multiples of input dimensions, check input-sized blocks and rotations/reflections first.
3. Before submission, construct the entire proposed output and compare every edit to the demos—not just to a plausible local visual pattern. A proposed fill, ray, or extension must be supported by observed behavior; do not infer direction, extent, or color from an isolated clue. Never infer correctness from one partial resemblance.
4. After an incorrect submission, treat feedback as whole-grid rejection only—not evidence about which cells were wrong. Identify the unsupported assumption and revise it; never repeat the same grid. If distinct rules still fit, spend a demo request only when its expected disambiguation is worth its cost under the remaining attempt/demo budget. Otherwise, make the best demo-consistent choice without pretending an unresolved guess is verified.
5. Keep the interaction action-only: choose exactly one legal action per turn and put its JSON object on the final line—submit a complete grid, request_demos, or finish only after the instance is over and finish is allowed. Do not add narration, speculation, or tool calls before the required JSON; use reasoning internally and validate the complete action before replying.
